Networks

How data gets from one device to another, step by step.

Why does a video call lag even on fast internet?

Practise this subject in Packet Valley

The big picture

  • Layers and protocolsWhy networks are split into layers, what a protocol is, and the two layer models you will meet.
  • EncapsulationHow each layer wraps the data from the layer above, and what that wrapping costs.
  • Services and interfacesWhat a layer offers to the layer above it, and the set of calls a program uses to ask for it.

Wires and signals

  • DelayThe four kinds of delay a packet meets, and why a faster plan does not always make things feel faster.
  • Cables and wirelessThe main ways a signal travels between devices, and what each one is good for.
  • Signals and bandwidthHow bits become a signal on a wire, and what bandwidth means in hertz and in bits a second.
  • Channel limitsThe two limits on how fast a channel can carry data, from the number of signal levels and from noise.
  • Sharing a linkHow many conversations use one link at the same time, by splitting it up by time, by frequency, or by packet.

Frames and errors

  • FramingHow a stream of bits is cut into frames, and how a frame marks where it starts and ends.
  • Error detectionHow a receiver can tell that bits were damaged on the way, using parity bits and checksums.
  • CRCHow a cyclic redundancy check uses a special kind of division to catch errors that a checksum would miss.
  • Error correctionHow extra bits let a receiver fix a damaged bit by itself, using a small Hamming code.
  • Sliding windowsHow a sender keeps several frames in flight at once, and why that keeps a long link busy.

Sharing the channel

  • ALOHAThe simplest way to share a channel, where anyone sends whenever they like, and how often that works.
  • Carrier senseHow listening before sending, and backing off after a collision, makes Ethernet far better than ALOHA.
  • Taking turnsHow stations share a channel by passing a turn around, with no collisions, and what that costs.
  • Hidden terminalsWhy two Wi-Fi devices can collide without hearing each other, and how a short request-and-reply fixes it.
  • Ethernet and switchesWhat an Ethernet frame holds, and how a switch learns where each device is.

Addresses and routes

  • Forwarding and routingThe difference between moving one packet along and working out the routes, and how a router picks a row in its table.
  • IP addressesWhat an IP address is, how IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are written, and a few addresses with special jobs.
  • SubnettingHow one network is split into smaller ones, and how to tell which one an address belongs to.
  • FragmentationWhat happens when a packet is too big for a link, and how fragments are labelled so they can be put back together.
  • Shortest-path routingHow a router works out the cheapest route to every other router when it knows the whole map, using Dijkstra's algorithm.
  • Distance-vector routingHow routers that only talk to their neighbours still learn the best routes, and what goes wrong when a link fails.
  • Announcing routesHow separate networks on the internet tell each other which addresses they can reach, using BGP and AS paths.

Ports and transport

  • Ports and UDPHow port numbers get data to the right program, and how UDP sends data with no set-up and no repeats.
  • The TCP handshakeHow two computers agree to talk before any data is sent, and what each of the three messages says.
  • TCP reliabilityHow TCP numbers bytes, confirms what arrived, and resends what did not.
  • Windows and timersHow TCP limits how much the receiver has to hold, and how it works out how long to wait before resending.
  • Congestion controlHow TCP slows down when the network is crowded, and how it speeds up again.

The web and email

  • DNSHow a name like example.com is turned into an IP address, and why the answer is saved along the way.
  • HTTP and the webHow a browser asks a server for a page, what the request and reply look like, and what the status codes mean.
  • Cookies and cachingHow a site remembers you between requests with cookies, and how saved copies make pages load faster.
  • EmailHow a message travels from one mailbox to another, and which protocol does which part.
  • StreamingHow video and music play while they download, and how the player picks a quality that your connection can keep up with.

Security

  • Network security basicsThe ideas behind keeping messages private and knowing who sent them, and what the padlock in your browser does and does not mean.
  • Ciphers and secret keysHow a message is scrambled with a secret key, why simple ciphers fail, and the one rule every good cipher follows.
  • Block ciphersHow modern encryption works on fixed-size blocks, why the mode matters, and what AES is.
  • Public-key cryptographyHow two people who have never met can share secrets, shown with a small RSA example you can check by hand.
  • Signatures and certificatesHow a signature proves who sent something, and how a chain of certificates lets your browser trust a website's key.
  • FirewallsHow a firewall decides which traffic may pass, using rules checked in order, and why a default of deny is the safe choice.
